$comment: Tunable weights for the expected-points (xPts) heuristic. Every number that shapes a
projection lives here, not in code, so the model can be re-tuned without a rebuild.
modelVersion is stamped onto every stored projection, and calibration only ever learns from
projections made under the CURRENT version - so bumping it throws away the grading history.
That makes the rule for bumping narrow and important: bump it when the numbers that produce
xPts change, and only then. Captaincy, chip timing, transfer logic and anything else that
reads a projection without altering it must NOT bump it. Those decisions are not stamped on
the projection and a correction learned under one is perfectly valid under the next.
0.18.0, 0.19.0 and 0.20.0 broke that rule: all three changed captaincy or chip timing and
left xPts identical, and each one reset the learning to zero for no reason. That is why the
Accuracy page kept saying it had nothing to learn from yet after three graded gameweeks.
status codes: a=available, d=doubtful, i=injured, s=suspended, u=unavailable, n=not in squad.
chance_of_playing_next_round, when the API supplies it, is authoritative and overrides the
status default - a 75% flagged player is weighted 0.75.
Expected minutes drive appearance points and scale every other component.
Recent starts are blended with the season rate, then shrunk toward a prior so a
one-match sample cannot produce a confident projection.
lowOwnershipThreshold/lowOwnershipStartCap: below that ownership percent, every other
manager's team news and press-conference reading is stronger evidence than our own start
count, so the start probability is capped there regardless of what a stray appearance -
an injury-cover start, a dead-rubber cameo - suggested. This is what stops a 0.1%-owned
third-choice goalkeeper being projected as though he were nailed on.
rotationRiskRestDaysThreshold/rotationRiskDiscount: a club playing again this soon after
its last fixture is most often a European tie sandwiched between two league gameweeks -
the only reason top-flight fixtures get shuffled this tight. The FPL API carries no
European fixtures at all, so a short gap between two Premier League ones is the signal.
ownershipPriorPivot/ownershipPriorMax: the start prior is set by ownership - the crowd's
aggregated team news - rather than being a flat number for everyone. A flat prior after one
match gave a nailed-on 70%-owned striker and a 2%-owned fringe defender the identical 51%
start chance, which flattened every early-season projection into the same narrow band and
filled defences with players who were not in the first XI. Same evidence lowOwnershipThreshold
already trusts over our own start count, used as a two-sided signal instead of only a cap.
Converts bootstrap team strength ratings into expected goals for and against.
Expected goals = leagueAverage * (attack/opponentDefence)^exponent * venue factor.
tableWeight/formPriorMatches: current form nudges those ratings, separately for attack and
defence, and from EXPECTED goals rather than results. It used to be one points-per-game
number applied to both, which is the most luck-exposed metric in the game - a defence that
has conceded nothing off five expected goals against reads as the best in the league on
points alone, and one number cannot describe a side scoring freely while leaking badly.
Expected goals stabilise far faster, which is exactly why attacking.xgWeight already
prefers them for players; this applies the same belief to clubs.
tableWeight 1.0: the shrunk ratio is used as it stands. At 0.3 it was a SECOND damp on
an estimate the sample-size shrinkage had already damped, and two mechanisms for the
same doubt multiplied together produce inert rather than careful. Measured: a club
creating half the league average, six matches in, was downgraded 9.1% - 0.61 points on
a 6.7 projection - while the fixture alone moved the same player 61% between his best
and worst week. The model knew which games were hard and had no idea which clubs had
stopped scoring, because strength came from pre-season ratings: reputation, not form.
formPriorMatches 5: two matches of underlying numbers is barely more evidence than two
matches of results, so form is shrunk toward no adjustment until a real sample exists.
Bounded to 0.7-1.3 either way, so form nudges the API's ratings and never replaces them.
fixtureBaseline: what a fixture's expected goals are compared AGAINST when scaling a
player's attacking rate. 'league' divides by the league average, which double counts club
strength: a strong club's attacker already earned his rate per 90 while playing for that
strong club, and dividing his club's expected goals by the league average credits him for
it a second time. Measured on the model's own constants, against a league-average opponent
at home, a strong club's attacker is scaled 1.29 and a weak club's 0.96 - an 18% spread
that is nothing to do with the fixture. 'club' divides by that club's OWN typical output
instead, leaving the scalar measuring only what it is for: this opponent, and this venue.
'league' is the default until the ablation says otherwise, because switching it changes
xPts and so resets the self-correction.
Per-90 attacking rates. xG/xA are preferred where the API supplies them because they
stabilise far faster than raw goals; xgWeight blends the two. Rates are then scaled by
how good the fixture looks relative to an average one.
priorWeightMinutes: how many minutes of evidence it takes to half-trust a per-90 rate -
shared by every category (goals, assists, saves, defensive contribution, bonus), not just
attacking ones. 900 (ten matches) rather than a shorter, weaker prior because a goal is a
rare, high-value, high-variance event: one goal in one early match is nowhere near enough
evidence that a player has a real, repeatable scoring threat.
lowThreatPriorWeightMinutes: a stronger prior again, applied only to goal involvement for a
GKP or DEF. One shared prior cannot be right for both a striker (whose true rate is
genuinely close to it) and a defender (whose true rate is close to zero) at once - even
900 minutes was not enough to stop a defender's one gameweek 1 goal outranking Haaland's
whole season-to-date output for gameweek 2's captaincy. 2700 (thirty matches) means a
defender needs a real, sustained run of goal involvement before it counts for much.
anchorPriorWeightMinutes/positionBaselineRates: the anchor a thin rate shrinks toward is
itself a rate with a sample size, and it has to earn its weight the same way everything
else here does. Anchoring to last season was right; taking that anchor at face value
however few minutes it came from was not - two goals in 200 minutes read as a proven
0.9-per-90 threat, and priorWeightMinutes then asserted it with the weight of ten full
matches. The anchor is now shrunk over 900 minutes toward what an ordinary player in that
position does per 90. An established scorer keeps almost all of his rate; a player with a
cameo season keeps almost none of it and falls back to ordinary-for-his-position, which is
a far better guess than either the cameo or zero.

cleanSheet.$comment: P(clean sheet) = exp(-expected goals conceded), a Poisson zero, capped for sanity.

saves.$comment: Goalkeeper saves scale with how much the opponent is expected to shoot.

$comment: P(hitting the DefCon threshold) from the player's per-90 CBIT/CBIRT rate via a logistic.
steepness controls how sharply probability rises once a player's rate passes the threshold.
If the API does not expose a usable per-90 defensive stat, fallbackProbability is used and
the projection is flagged as low-confidence rather than silently scoring zero.

bonus.$comment: Expected bonus points from the player's historical bonus rate per 90, damped toward zero.

$comment: Who takes the penalties. The API has published it all along; nothing read it until now.
newPenaltyTakerGoalsPerMatch 0: OFF by default, and that is the whole point. A player's
expected goals ALREADY contain the penalties he has taken, so an uplift on top double
counts for every settled taker - nearly all of them. The case history cannot describe is
the taker appointed recently: his own record excludes the pens he is now going to take,
and will go on excluding them for weeks.
That case is detectable because set-piece duty is stored per snapshot, so a player who
is first choice now and was not in the oldest snapshot held is newly appointed. The
uplift applies to him and to nobody else.
A sensible value is about 0.10 goals a match: roughly five penalties per club per season
over 38 matches, times the share that are scored. At MID scoring that is half a point a
match, which is the right order - enough to separate two similar attackers, nowhere near
enough to overturn a real difference.
It stays at 0 until the ablation on the Accuracy page says it earns its place. Turning it
on changes xPts and so bumps modelVersion, which resets the self-correction - and that
correction is worth more than this is.
Open decision D4, resolved: mostly maximise points, with a mild tiebreak toward rank.
Players owned by less than ownershipPivot percent of managers get a small xPts bonus,
scaled by weight. At weight 0.15 the largest possible bonus (a 0%-owned player) is 0.15
xPts - small enough to only ever decide a genuinely close call, never to justify picking a
meaningfully worse player just for being different. Set to 0 to go back to pure
expected-points maximisation; raise it to chase mini-league rank more aggressively.
What top-ranked managers actually own, sampled from public league standings. Squads are
private until a gameweek starts, so this is zero for every projection before then - that
is a platform limit, not a bug. Once sampled, elite ownership nudges xPts up (never down:
the absence of elite ownership this early is not evidence against a player), with an extra
nudge for players the elite sample is actually captaining.
weight is per 100% elite ownership; captainWeight is per 100% of the sample captaining.
Selection-time risk discount, by confidence tier. Two players projected at the same xPts
are not equally trustworthy - a proven, high-confidence starter should beat a speculative
low-confidence punt scoring the same on paper, because the punt's number is more likely to
be wrong in either direction. This only affects which players the solver picks; the xPts
shown on the page, and the number graded for accuracy, are always the undiscounted figure.
1.0 = no discount.
How far ahead transfers, captaincy and squad-building look, beyond the single gameweek
being planned for. length 5, decay 0.75: the target week counts fully, the next 0.75, then
0.56, 0.42, 0.32 - a fixture swing three or four weeks out still matters, but far less than
the week right in front of you. captainConsistencyWeight is a small, bounded, upward-only
nudge toward a captain who is strong across the whole horizon rather than spiking in just
this one week. benchBoostRelief relaxes how harshly a squad discounts its bench when a
double gameweek sits within the horizon, so bench depth is not neglected right up until
the week it would be worth boosting - bounded well short of treating bench like starters.
wildcardLength 8: a Wildcard squad is kept far longer than a single transfer is, so it is
judged over a longer run. At decay 0.75 the extra weeks carry 0.24, 0.18 and 0.13, so this
does not swamp the near term - it lets a fixture swing two months out register at all,
which at length 5 it could not. Free Hit and ordinary transfers keep length 5, because
what they commit you to really does end sooner.
futureDiscountPerGameweek: how much less a chip's value counts for in a future gameweek
than in this one, when deciding when to play it. Ranking purely on projected gain treats a
projection thirteen weeks out as exactly as trustworthy as one for this week, and it is
not: fixtures move, strength ratings drift, and the player may be injured, rotated, or no
longer in your squad. A banked chip is worth its projection multiplied by the chance the
plan survives that long.
This is not horizon.decay. That discounts future points because sooner is better; this
discounts future *claims* because distant ones are weaker evidence.
0.97: four weeks out keeps 89%, thirteen weeks keeps 67%. Gentle on purpose - it breaks a
near-tie toward acting on what you can see, and a genuinely better future week still wins.
Set to 1.0 to rank purely on gain, which is exactly the older behaviour.
indistinguishableMargin 0.75: how far clear of the next-best week a chip has to be before
the model claims it found the right week at all. A chip is worth one play a season, and
playing it on a week that cannot be told apart from three others throws it away for
nothing. Below this margin the advice says so plainly instead of presenting an arbitrary
pick as a finding.
wildcardBeatenMargin 0.5: a Wildcard is valued on how many of your fifteen the best
affordable squad BEATS, not on how many it merely swaps. The optimal squad differs from
almost any real one in eight or nine places, so counting differences would advise a
Wildcard every week of the season. Half a point per player is a gap worth paying a
transfer for, and small enough not to miss a real rebuild.
wildcardMinTransfers 4: below this many beaten players, ordinary transfers get there.
One free transfer a week and -4 beyond it means three moves cost 8 points in one week
or three weeks of waiting - both cheaper than a chip worth one play a season.
The captain scores double and the Triple Captain chip trebles once a season, which makes
both the wrong decisions to take on an average alone. Two players projected at 9.0 are not
the same bet when one has a real chance of fifteen and the other reliably returns 8-10.
ceilingWeight 0.1 with maxCeilingBonus 1.25, applied to how much upside a player carries
beyond his own mean rather than to the raw ceiling - the raw ceiling correlates so strongly
with expected points that using it directly would just be a second, noisier vote for the
same thing. Capped deliberately: a ceiling breaks a tie between similar bets, it never
justifies taking a worse one.
tiebreakEpsilon is the vice-captain sort's definition of near-equal. That comparison used
to sit behind a || that short-circuits only on exactly zero, so ceilingWeight was dead
config affecting nothing at all.
haulThreshold 10: a double-figure return is what a captaincy is actually trying to catch.
The cap was 0.6 and that was a fault, not caution: measured over the shapes that compete
for the armband it squashed an eight-point spread of real upside into 0.15 points of bonus
and pinned both premium forwards - the players the term exists to find - at the same value.
1.25 is the model's own measured typical miss. A gap in expected points smaller than that
is not evidence, so upside decides inside roughly that band and nowhere beyond it.
tooCloseMargin 1.0: display only. A captaincy doubles one score, so a gap smaller than
this is not a finding - it is two similar bets, and the page says so rather than dressing
an arbitrary winner as a verdict. Never changes who is captained.
tripleCaptainUsesCeiling applies that same bounded bonus to Triple Captain timing. It used
to rank gameweeks on the raw ceiling, which was wrong: a 90th percentile of a discrete
distribution saturates, so a double gameweek raised the captain's expected gain far more
than it raised his ceiling, and ranking on the ceiling discarded most of the reason a
double gameweek is the week you want. Same rule as the captaincy now - upside separates
near-equal weeks, it never overturns a clearly better one.
How much a bench place is worth when choosing a squad. A benched player only scores
through auto-subs, so they are worth far less than a starter - but not nothing, which is
why a squad optimiser that ignored the bench would happily field four unplayable
reserves. The backup keeper is worth least of all.
startRiskWeight: an extra discount for a player who may not be on the pitch at all, on top
of the expected minutes xPts already includes. Expected value alone is the wrong basis for
an XI slot - a 20%-to-start player is not a fifth of a player, he is overwhelmingly likely
to return nothing, and the slot cannot be recovered. 0 disables it, 1 applies it in full.
priorityFixXPtsThreshold: below this many points for the gameweek, a squad member is
treated as a dead slot regardless of how the raw numbers rank - see findTransfers() in
src/report/recommend.ts. 1.0 sits well below a normal fringe player's projection (bench
players with a genuine game to come typically project 1.5-2+) and comfortably above a
backup goalkeeper or an unused-substitute's near-zero projection.
timingNoteRatio: purely informational, never a recommendation to wait or a scoring change -
see transferTimingNoteFor(). 0.6 means a note appears once this gameweek's projection is
below 60% of the target's own average across the rest of the horizon, or above 1/0.6 of it -
either way, their value is concentrated well away from an even spread across the run.
A soft, informational note only - never an xPts adjustment, never a gate on selection.
FPL's real price-change algorithm is unpublished, so this is not a prediction of exactly
when a price will move, only a 'worth knowing' flag. Ranks every player by net transfers
this gameweek (in minus out) and flags the topN at each end, but only when net transfers
clear netTransfersFloor - otherwise a quiet gameweek's top 20 is really just noise.
Correcting the model with its own measured error, per position. The accuracy tables have
always computed bias per position and nothing has ever read it; this is what does.
priorWeightPlayers 400: bias over a single gameweek is mostly that week's own variance, so
a position needs a few hundred graded projections before its lean is believable.
minGameweeks 3: below that there is no lean to speak of, only noise.
minFactor/maxFactor 0.8/1.25: a model needing more correction than that has a bug to be
found, not a lean to be tuned out, and silently applying a bigger one would hide it.
The factor is always measured against the uncalibrated projection, never against already-
corrected output - see projection.xpts_uncalibrated. Measuring a working correction against
its own corrected output concludes it is no longer needed and reverts it.
Set enabled to false to project exactly as if none of this existed.
